newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan government warns embassies over protest.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan government warns embassies over protest.

text.p: Kenya's government told foreign embassies on Thursday to respect diplomatic protocol after a sharp and collective protest about political freedoms by the U.S., European Union and Japanese envoys.

In their joint statement on Wednesday the 14 embassies, who represent all Kenya's important donors, deplored recent police actions and called for free speech and assembly ahead of this year's elections.

Foreign Minister Kalonzo Musyoka replied on Thursday the government was gravely concerned embassies were returning to the public, confrontational style of former U.S. ambassador Smith Hempstone before Kenya's first multi-party polls in 1992.
The foreign protest was evidence that donors, led by the United States, are stepping up the pressure on President Daniel arap Moi to ensure political reforms keep pace with economic liberalisation.
The public rebuke coincided with a visit to Nairobi by a senior International Monetary Fund (IMF) official to review progress on privatisation and other issues.
The embassies urged the government to allow political leaders, candidates and citizens freedom of speech and assembly because they were vital to free and fair elections.

"Political leaders and candidates of all persuasions should be able to freely meet and address the citizens of Kenya so that voters have the information necessary to make informed choices when they exercise their right to vote," the statement said.
Moi and his ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) are clear favourites to win presidential and parliamentary elections due to be held by the end of 1997.
The only threat to the victory would come if the opposition leaders put personal and tribal rivalries aside and unite behind a single candidate against Moi, political analysts say.

The embassies deplored the disruption of peaceful opposition meetings over the past week and hit out at the shooting of the bodyguard of an official leader of the opposition in parliament. Two policemen have appeared in court charged with wounding the guard.
The statement was issued by the embassies of Austria, Belgium, Britain, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and the United States.
"The sentiments have indeed been noted," Musyoka said on Thursday. He said the government did not intend to suppress the opposition but the police force would enforce the law.
He said it was normal practice for foreign embassies to raise their concerns with the government instead of going public with them, which amounted to a challenge to Kenyan sovereignty.
"We cannot be seen to compromise on national sovereignty," said Musyoka, adding that any ambassadors who totally ignored diplomatic protocol and principles would not be permitted.
"They could have brought a protest note to me," he said. "They should refrain from falling into opposition traps." He said all public gatherings in Kenya by law required a licence.
The opposition, human rights groups and some embassies argue that the licences are seldom given to the opposition.
